transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um, yeah, thanks. I'm here because... well, for almost two years now, I've been dealing with this situation. I'm a music director, and after this one commission I did, I just haven't been able to shake the certainty that a few people in my ensemble are quietly trying to undermine my work. 

They do it through, like, sudden schedule changes, or specific seating choices, and just... little comments during rehearsals. And even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, I know what they're actually doing. It's just been going on for a long time, so I figured I should come in and talk to someone about it.
Aside from these suspicions about your colleagues, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice?

No, um... no, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see things, if that's what you're asking. I mean, my hearing is obviously very trained for my work, but I'm not hearing sounds that aren't there. It's really just the actual things happening in the ensemble—the things they actually do and say to me. So, no, I haven't noticed anything like what you're describing.

Outside of this situation with your ensemble, do you generally find yourself suspicious or mistrustful of other people in your life—like friends, family, or people you meet in other settings—and has that been a pattern for you since you were younger?

Um, no, not at all. I actually trust my friends and my family completely. I've never really been a suspicious person, even when I was younger... I'd say I'm usually pretty trusting, actually. 

It's really just... it's just this specific situation with those few people in the ensemble. Outside of work, I don't have any issues trusting people I meet or anything like that.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F60.0 given absence of lifelong pervasive distrust/suspiciousness (patient reports trusting friends/family, no premorbid pattern). Ruled out F20.0 and F28 given absence of hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms and a single, circumscribed, non-bizarre delusional belief system persisting ~2 years, consistent with delusional disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory belief (colleagues undermining his work) persisting for nearly two years, encapsulated to a specific context (his ensemble) rather than pervasive. He explicitly denies hallucinations or other perceptual disturbances, ruling out schizophrenia. He also denies a lifelong pattern of generalized distrust/suspiciousness toward others (friends, family, general acquaintances), which argues against paranoid personality disorder. The circumscribed nature of the delusion, absence of hallucinations, absence of prodromal negative symptoms, and preserved trust in other relationships are consistent with Delusional Disorder, persecutory type.
